title: What does ILO Convention 190 require on harassment training, and which countries have ratified it?
description: ILO Convention 190 on violence and harassment: the Article 9(d) training duty, Recommendation 206, and ratification status in five markets.
shortAnswer: The International Labour Organization's Violence and Harassment Convention, 2019 (No. 190) requires ratifying States to adopt laws obliging employers to give workers information and training on identified violence and harassment risks, prevention measures, and their rights under the workplace policy (Article 9(d)). As at November 2026, NORMLEX lists Australia and Portugal as ratifying States with the Convention in force; Japan, the United States and the United Arab Emirates have not ratified.
keyTakeaways: Convention 190 binds States, not employers directly. Employers feel it through national laws that ratifying States must adopt under Article 9.

Article 9(d) is the training clause: employers must provide workers and other persons concerned with "information and training, in accessible formats as appropriate" on hazards, risks, and prevention and protection measures.
The Convention entered into force on June 25, 2021. NORMLEX listed 56 ratifications as at November 2026.
Australia ratified on June 9, 2023 and Portugal on February 16, 2024; both are shown as in force. Japan, the United States and the UAE do not appear in the ratification list.
Recommendation No. 206 is not binding but describes what a good workplace policy and training program contain, including protection for whistle-blowers and attention to third-party risks.
jurisdiction: International: International Labour Organization (ILO), with ratification status for Australia, Portugal, Japan, the United States and the United Arab Emirates
regulator: International Labour Organization (ILO) supervisory bodies; obligations are implemented by each ratifying member State through national law
appliesTo: ILO member States that have ratified the Convention, which must legislate and supervise
Employers in ratifying States, through national laws adopted under Article 9

Workers and others in the world of work: employees, persons in training including interns and apprentices, volunteers, jobseekers, job applicants, and individuals exercising employer authority (Article 2(1))
All sectors, public or private, formal or informal, urban or rural (Article 2(2))

sections.heading: What is Convention 190 and who is bound by it?

blocks.text: Convention 190 is an international labor treaty that binds only the ILO member States that ratify it. It was adopted in Geneva on June 21, 2019 at the 108th (Centenary) Session of the International Labour Conference, and entered into force on June 25, 2021. Under [Article 14](https://normlex.ilo.org/dyn/nrmlx_en/f?p=NORMLEXPUB:12100:0::NO::P12100_ILO_CODE:C190), it comes into force for each ratifying State twelve months after its ratification is registered.

An employer cannot be sanctioned under the Convention itself. Its effect on employers comes through Article 12, which says the Convention is applied through national laws and regulations, collective agreements, and "extending or adapting existing occupational safety and health measures". That is why the national pages linked below matter more for day to day compliance than the treaty text.

Article 1 defines violence and harassment broadly as unacceptable behaviors and practices, "whether a single occurrence or repeated", that aim at, result in, or are likely to result in physical, psychological, sexual or economic harm, including gender-based violence and harassment. Article 3 extends the world of work to commuting, work-related travel and training, employer-provided accommodation, and "work-related communications, including those enabled by information and communication technologies".

sections.heading: What does the Convention say about training?

blocks.text: Training appears at three levels: a duty States must place on employers, a State policy duty, and a State support duty. The employer-facing clause is Article 9, which requires each ratifying State to adopt laws requiring employers to take appropriate steps commensurate with their degree of control, "so far as is reasonably practicable", to:

items: adopt and implement, in consultation with workers and their representatives, a workplace policy on violence and harassment (Article 9(a));
take violence and harassment and associated psychosocial risks into account in occupational safety and health management (Article 9(b));
identify hazards and assess the risks, with worker participation, and take measures to prevent and control them (Article 9(c)); and

provide workers and other persons concerned with "information and training, in accessible formats as appropriate, on the identified hazards and risks of violence and harassment and the associated prevention and protection measures, including on the rights and responsibilities of workers and other persons concerned in relation to the policy" (Article 9(d)).

blocks.text: At State level, Article 4(2)(g) includes "developing tools, guidance, education and training, and raising awareness" in the inclusive approach every ratifying State must adopt. Article 11(b) asks States to ensure employers, workers, their organizations and authorities are provided with "guidance, resources, training or other tools" on violence and harassment.

blocks.title: Reading Article 9(d)
blocks.text: The training must be tied to the risks the employer has actually identified under Article 9(c), not a generic course. It must also cover the rights and responsibilities in the employer's own policy under Article 9(a). A training program that does not reference the risk assessment or the policy is weak evidence that Article 9(d) has been implemented.

The [Violence and Harassment Recommendation, 2019 (No. 206)](https://normlex.ilo.org/dyn/nrmlx_en/f?p=NORMLEXPUB:12100:0::NO::P12100_ILO_CODE:R206) supplements the Convention and is not open to ratification. It gives the content detail a training designer needs.

items: **Paragraph 7:** the workplace policy should state that violence and harassment will not be tolerated, set out prevention programs with measurable objectives where appropriate, specify rights and responsibilities, describe complaint and investigation procedures, address privacy and confidentiality, and protect "complainants, victims, witnesses and whistle-blowers against victimization or retaliation".

**Paragraph 8:** the risk assessment should consider psychosocial hazards and risks from working conditions, from third parties such as "clients, customers, service providers, users, patients and members of the public", and from discrimination and abuse of power relations.

**Paragraph 9:** sectors where exposure may be more likely include night work, work in isolation, health, hospitality, social services, emergency services, domestic work, transport, education and entertainment.
**Paragraph 20:** labor inspectors and other officials should undergo gender-responsive training.
**Paragraph 23(b) and (c):** States should develop gender-responsive training programs to assist employers and workers, and model codes of practice and risk assessment tools.

sections.heading: Which of the five markets have ratified Convention 190?

blocks.text: Two of the five markets have ratified. The table reflects the [NORMLEX ratification list for C190](https://normlex.ilo.org/dyn/nrmlx_en/f?p=NORMLEXPUB:11300:0::NO::P11300_INSTRUMENT_ID:3999810) as at November 2026, which showed 56 ratifications and no denunciations.

blocks.text: Within the European Union, NORMLEX lists ratifications by several Member States, including Austria, Belgium, Cyprus, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Portugal, Romania and Spain. Slovenia ratified on April 30, 2026, and NORMLEX notes the Convention will enter into force for it on April 30, 2027. The EU itself is not a party, since ILO conventions are ratified by States.

Non-ratification does not mean there is no harassment training duty. Japan, the United States and the UAE all have domestic rules, covered on pages such as [Japan's power harassment prevention obligations](/regulations/japan-power-harassment-prevention-obligations) and [state sexual harassment training requirements](/regulations/state-sexual-harassment-training-requirements). For Australia and Portugal, see the [positive duty on sexual harassment](/regulations/positive-duty-sexual-harassment-training) and [Portugal's workplace harassment prevention obligations](/regulations/portugal-workplace-harassment-prevention-obligations).

sections.heading: How should a multinational design training around Convention 190?

blocks.text: Use the Convention as a common baseline and national law as the binding layer. A practical sequence:

items: List the countries of operation, mark which have ratified C190 on NORMLEX, and identify the national law that implements it or applies regardless.
Run the Article 9(c) risk assessment per site, including third-party risks from customers or patients and risks in remote and online work under Article 3(d).
Write training content from the assessment and the policy, so each module references real risks and real reporting routes.
Cover everyone Article 2 protects, including interns, apprentices, volunteers and contractors, and provide accessible formats as Article 9(d) requires.
Train managers and investigators separately on complaint handling, confidentiality and protection against retaliation.
Keep records that tie each completion to the policy version and risk assessment it was based on.

blocks.text: The method for linking each duty to a learning outcome is set out in [how to map training to compliance obligations](/guides/how-to-map-training-to-compliance-obligations), and psychosocial risk content is covered on the page about [psychosocial hazards training requirements](/regulations/psychosocial-hazards-training-requirements).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models the Convention's Article 9 duties as a shared baseline and attaches each country's implementing law as its own obligation set. A multinational can then see where one module satisfies several jurisdictions and where a country needs additional content.

faqs.q: Does Convention 190 apply to my company if my country has not ratified it?
faqs.a: Not as a legal obligation. ILO conventions bind States that ratify them, and employers are bound only by the national laws those States adopt. Many multinationals still use Article 9 as a group baseline because it aligns with harassment and safety rules in non-ratifying countries and simplifies a single global program.

faqs.q: How often must harassment training be repeated under Convention 190?
faqs.a: The Convention sets no frequency. Article 9(d) requires information and training on identified risks and prevention measures, which implies updating training when the risk assessment or policy changes. National law may set intervals, so the refresh cycle should follow the strictest jurisdiction that applies to each worker.

Yes. Article 3(d) covers violence and harassment occurring "through work-related communications, including those enabled by information and communication technologies". Training should therefore address chat, email, video meetings and social media used for work, as well as harassment during commuting and work-related travel.

faqs.q: When did the Convention come into force for Australia and Portugal?
faqs.a: Article 14(3) brings the Convention into force for a State twelve months after its ratification is registered. Australia's ratification is dated June 9, 2023 and Portugal's February 16, 2024, so it took effect for them in June 2024 and February 2025 respectively. NORMLEX lists both as in force.
